title: Explain the five SOLID principles with a concrete violation + fix for each — Single Responsibility (a class that validates, computes, persists, AND notifies changes for four different reasons → split it), Open/Closed (extend by adding a class, not editing an if/else-on-type chain), Liskov Substitution (a Square extends Rectangle whose overridden setWidth/setHeight break callers written for Rectangle → not substitutable), Interface Segregation (a fat Animal{eat,sleep,fly,swim} forces a Dog to throw UnsupportedOperationException on fly() → split into role interfaces Eater/Swimmer/Flyer), and Dependency Inversion (depend on an abstraction and inject the implementation, not a concrete class).
shortTitle: Explain the five SOLID principles with a violation and fix for each

s1_definition.profdef: SOLID is an acronym for five object-oriented design principles that lead to code that is easy to extend, test, and maintain. Single Responsibility says a class should have one reason to change. Open/Closed says software should be open for extension but closed for modification. Liskov Substitution says a subtype must be usable anywhere its supertype is expected without breaking correctness. Interface Segregation says clients should not depend on methods they do not use. Dependency Inversion says high-level modules should depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India each employee has one clearly defined job, which is Single Responsibility — the teller does not also audit and send SMS. When the bank adds a new loan product, it opens a new counter rather than rewriting the existing one, which is Open/Closed. A trainee manager must be able to stand in for any manager without confusing customers, which is Liskov. Employees only get the forms relevant to their role, not every form in the bank, which is Interface Segregation. And the branch depends on a general "payment processor" role rather than one named vendor, so it can swap vendors easily, which is Dependency Inversion.
s1_definition.oneliner: SOLID means one job per class, extend by adding not editing, subtypes must not break callers, keep interfaces small and role-based, and depend on abstractions you inject.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** SOLID is an acronym for five object-oriented design principles that lead to code that is easy to extend, test, and maintain. Single Responsibility says a class should have one reason to change. Open/Closed says software should be open for extension but closed for modification. Liskov Substitution says a subtype must be usable anywhere its supertype is expected without breaking correctness. Interface Segregation says clients should not depend on methods they do not use. Dependency Inversion says high-level modules should depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India each employee has one clearly defined job, which is Single Responsibility — the teller does not also audit and send SMS. When the bank adds a new loan product, it opens a new counter rather than rewriting the existing one, which is Open/Closed. A trainee manager must be able to stand in for any manager without confusing customers, which is Liskov. Employees only get the forms relevant to their role, not every form in the bank, which is Interface Segregation. And the branch depends on a general "payment processor" role rather than one named vendor, so it can swap vendors easily, which is Dependency Inversion.

**One line to remember:** SOLID means one job per class, extend by adding not editing, subtypes must not break callers, keep interfaces small and role-based, and depend on abstractions you inject.

sections.s2_technical:
Single Responsibility Principle means a class should change for exactly one reason. A class that validates a transfer, computes fees, saves to the database, and sends notifications changes for four different reasons, so a change to the SMS provider risks breaking validation. The fix is to split into a Validator, a FeeCalculator, a Repository, and a NotificationService, each with one reason to change.

Open/Closed Principle means you add new behavior by adding new code, not by editing tested code. A fee calculator with `if (type == EQUITY) ... else if (type == FX) ...` must be edited every time a new trade type appears, which risks breaking existing branches. The fix is a `FeeStrategy` interface with one implementation per type; adding a derivative fee means adding a class, leaving existing ones untouched.

Liskov Substitution Principle means a subtype must honor the contract of its supertype. The classic violation is `Square extends Rectangle`: a Rectangle lets you set width and height independently, but a Square overrides the setters to keep them equal, so code that sets width to 5 and height to 10 and expects area 50 gets 100 instead. The subtype silently broke the caller's assumption. The fix is to not model Square as a subtype of Rectangle; use a common `Shape` abstraction with an `area()` method instead.

Interface Segregation Principle means do not force a class to implement methods it does not need. A fat `Animal` interface with `eat`, `sleep`, `fly`, and `swim` forces a `Dog` to throw UnsupportedOperationException on `fly()`. The fix is small role interfaces — `Eater`, `Swimmer`, `Flyer` — so each class implements only what it truly does. In banking, a fat `Account` interface with `calculateInterest`, `checkOverdraft`, and `tradeStocks` would force a plain savings account to stub out trading; splitting into `InterestBearing`, `Overdraftable`, and `Tradable` fixes it.

Dependency Inversion Principle means high-level policy should depend on an abstraction, and the concrete detail should be injected. A `TransferService` that does `new EmailNotifier()` inside itself is welded to email and is hard to test. The fix is to depend on a `Notifier` interface and inject the implementation through the constructor: `new TransferService(notifier)`. Now you can inject a mock in tests or an SMS notifier in production without touching the service.

A senior nuance: these principles reinforce each other. Dependency Inversion plus Open/Closed is what makes the Strategy pattern powerful, and Interface Segregation makes Liskov easier because small contracts are easier to honor fully.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India had a single giant `TransferManager` class, and it caused constant pain. Each principle fixes one real problem the team hit.

Problem 1 — One class did everything. TransferManager validated the request, computed the fee, saved the accounts, and sent the SMS. When the SMS vendor changed, a developer accidentally broke validation because it all lived in one place. This is the Single Responsibility violation; the fix splits the work into focused classes.

Problem 2 — Fees were a growing if-else. Every new trade type meant editing the fee method and risking the existing branches. This is the Open/Closed violation; the fix is a FeeStrategy per type.

Problem 3 — A premium account subtype broke callers. A PremiumAccount overrode debit to silently apply a discount, so code that expected an exact debit of Rs.50,000 saw a different balance change. This is the Liskov violation; the fix keeps the debit contract intact.

Problem 4 — A fat account interface forced stubs. A plain savings account was forced to implement tradeStocks and threw an exception. This is the Interface Segregation violation; the fix splits into role interfaces.

Problem 5 — The service created its own notifier. TransferManager did new EmailNotifier internally, so tests could not stub it. This is the Dependency Inversion violation; the fix injects a Notifier abstraction.

The demo shows the fixed design: a thin TransferService that depends on injected abstractions, a FeeStrategy chosen by type, role interfaces, and a correct Liskov-safe account.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (SAV2001, Rs.1,000,000) transfers Rs.50,000 rent to Priya (CUR3001, Rs.250,000), with an equity fee strategy.

Step 1: The demo injects the collaborators into TransferService — a validator, an equity fee strategy, and an SMS notifier. The service holds references typed as abstractions, so it never knows the concrete SmsNotifier class. This is Dependency Inversion living in the constructor.

Step 2: `transfer` calls `validator.validate(from, amount)`. Because validation is a separate class with one responsibility, a change here cannot break fee logic or notification. This is Single Responsibility.

Step 3: `feeStrategy.fee(50000)` runs. The EquityFee returns Rs.50 (0.10 percent). If the bank later adds derivatives, a new DerivativeFee class is added and this code is untouched. This is Open/Closed.

Step 4: The service validates again for the total Rs.50,050, then debits Rajesh by the full total. Because Account's debit honors its contract exactly with no hidden override, the caller's expectation holds. This is Liskov safety.

Step 5: Priya is credited the transfer amount Rs.50,000. Rajesh's balance becomes Rs.949,950 and Priya's becomes Rs.300,000.

Step 6: The service calls `notifier.notify(...)`. Because it depends on the Notifier interface, the concrete SMS implementation sends the message, but a test could inject a fake. This again is Dependency Inversion.

Step 7: Final balances are logged. Each SOLID principle contributed to a design where any one concern can change without disturbing the others.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26 09:10:45 [INFO] Transferred Rs.50000 (fee Rs.50.0000) SAV2001->CUR3001
2026-10-26 09:10:45 [INFO] Dear Rajesh Kumar, Rs.50000 transferred.
2026-10-26 09:10:45 [INFO] Rajesh balance: Rs.949950.0000
2026-10-26 09:10:45 [INFO] Priya balance : Rs.300000
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
SOLID is five object-oriented design principles that together produce code that is easy to extend, test, and maintain. I explain each with the violation it prevents and the fix.

Single Responsibility means a class should have one reason to change. The violation is a TransferManager that validates, computes fees, persists, and notifies, because then a change to the SMS vendor can break validation. The fix is to split it into a Validator, a FeeCalculator, a Repository, and a NotificationService. Open/Closed means software should be open for extension but closed for modification. The violation is a growing if-else on trade type inside a fee method, which must be edited and retested for every new type. The fix is a FeeStrategy interface with one implementation per type, so a new type is a new class with no edits to existing code.

Liskov Substitution means a subtype must be usable anywhere its supertype is expected without breaking correctness. The classic violation is Square extending Rectangle, where overriding the setters to keep sides equal breaks any caller that sets width and height independently and expects a rectangle's area. The fix is to not force that inheritance and instead use a common Shape abstraction with an area method. Interface Segregation means clients should not depend on methods they do not use. The violation is a fat Animal interface with fly and swim that forces a Dog to throw UnsupportedOperationException on fly. The fix is small role interfaces like Eater, Swimmer, and Flyer. In banking I split a fat account interface into InterestBearing and Tradable so a plain savings account is not forced to stub out trading.

Dependency Inversion means high-level modules depend on abstractions, not concrete classes, and the implementation is injected. The violation is a TransferService that does new EmailNotifier inside itself, which welds it to email and makes it untestable. The fix is to depend on a Notifier interface and inject the implementation through the constructor, so I can inject a mock in tests or swap SMS for email in production. In my settlement service at the National Bank of India this is exactly how it is built, and the payoff is that any one concern can change without disturbing the others, which is the whole reason SOLID exists.
